# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**ARIES-style physiological logging.** ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics, Mohan et al. 1992) logs *physiological* records: physical addressing to a page, logical description of the intra-page change. Every log record carries a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number (LSN)**; every buffer page carries a **pageLSN** recording the last update applied to it. The WAL protocol invariant is: a dirty page may not be flushed until all log records up to its pageLSN are durable (steal policy made safe), and a transaction may not report commit until its commit record is forced (no-force policy made safe). Undo actions are themselves logged as **Compensation Log Records (CLRs)** carrying an **undoNextLSN**, making undo idempotent and bounding repeated-crash work.

**Group commit.** Forcing the log on every commit serializes throughput on fsync latency. Group commit batches the commit records of many concurrent transactions into a single log force; a committing transaction waits briefly so that one `fsync`/`fdatasync` amortizes across the group. InnoDB implements this with a staged leader–follower design (flush/sync stages); PostgreSQL exposes `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings`. The durability contract is unchanged—commit is acknowledged only after the shared flush covers the transaction's commit LSN.

**Torn-page protection: full-page writes vs. the doublewrite buffer.** Because the device atomic write unit (often 4 KiB sector) is smaller than a database page (8–16 KiB), a crash mid-write can leave a *torn page* that physiological redo cannot repair. PostgreSQL uses **full-page writes (FPW)**: the first modification of a page after each checkpoint logs the entire page image, so redo restores a consistent base. InnoDB instead uses the **doublewrite buffer**: pages are first written sequentially to a dedicated area, fsynced, then written in place; recovery detects a torn in-place copy via checksums and restores from the doublewrite copy.

**Checkpointing interaction.** Fuzzy checkpoints record the Dirty Page Table and Active Transaction Table (with recLSNs) without quiescing writes, bounding the redo scan start point (the min recLSN) — detailed further in §8.

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**PostgreSQL heap-based tuple versioning.** Each heap tuple stores **xmin** (creating transaction ID) and **xmax** (deleting/updating XID). An update creates a new tuple version linked via **t_ctid**; visibility is decided against a transaction **snapshot** (xmin horizon, xmax, in-progress XID list) plus commit status from the CLOG (pg_xact). Dead versions are reclaimed by **VACUUM**, which also performs **transaction-ID freezing** to prevent 32-bit XID wraparound; **HOT (Heap-Only Tuple)** updates avoid index churn when indexed columns are unchanged.

**InnoDB undo-log-based MVCC.** InnoDB updates rows *in place* and writes before-images into **undo logs** in **rollback segments**. Each record carries DB_TRX_ID and DB_ROLL_PTR; a reader with a **read view** (snapshot of active trx IDs at REPEATABLE READ) walks the roll-pointer chain to reconstruct the version visible to it. The **purge** threads garbage-collect undo records once no read view can need them—long-running transactions therefore cause **history list length** growth, the analogue of Postgres bloat.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain snapshot isolation admits **write skew** (two transactions reading overlapping data and writing disjoint items, violating a constraint). SSI (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; shipped in PostgreSQL 9.1) tracks **rw-antidependencies** via SIREAD predicate locks and aborts a transaction when it detects a *dangerous structure*: two consecutive rw-antidependency edges (T1 →rw T2 →rw T3) with the pivot's neighbors concurrently committed—a conservative test for a cycle in the serialization graph.

**Timestamp-ordered in-memory MVCC (Hekaton).** Microsoft Hekaton assigns begin/end timestamps to versions; readers use a begin timestamp, writers install versions optimistically and validate at commit (read-set revalidation for serializability), with lock-free Bw-tree/hash indexes—showing MVCC decoupled from buffer-pool architecture.

## 3. LSM Trees (Log-Structured Merge Trees)

**Memtable → SSTable flush pipeline.** Writes go to a WAL (for durability) and an in-memory **memtable** (typically a skiplist, as in RocksDB/LevelDB). When full, it becomes an immutable memtable and is flushed as a sorted, immutable **SSTable** with a sparse index block. Deletes are logical **tombstones** that must survive until compaction can prove no older version exists beneath them (Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds` additionally guards against resurrecting deleted data on nodes that missed the delete).

**Compaction strategies: leveled vs. size-tiered.** **Leveled compaction** (RocksDB/LevelDB) keeps each level L_i as non-overlapping key ranges with exponentially growing capacity (~10×); compaction merges one SSTable from L_i into overlapping tables of L_{i+1}. It minimizes **space amplification** (~1.1×) and read amplification (one table per level) at the cost of high **write amplification** (~10 per level). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS)** merges similarly sized runs, giving low write amplification but high space/read amplification due to overlapping runs. **RocksDB universal compaction** and the **Dostoevsky/lazy-leveling** work (Dayan & Idreos) formalize the tiering↔leveling continuum per level.

**Bloom filters and fence pointers.** Each SSTable carries a **Bloom filter** over its keys so point lookups skip runs with high probability (false-positive rate tunable via bits/key; **Monkey** (Dayan et al. 2017) derives optimal non-uniform per-level filter allocation). **Fence pointers** (block index: first key of each data block) confine a lookup within a run to one block read. Together, point-read amplification approaches O(1) I/O despite many runs; range scans still pay a per-run merge cost, which is why leveling favors scan-heavy workloads.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Node splits, merges, and Structure Modification Operations (SMOs).** Insert into a full leaf triggers a **split**: half the entries move to a new sibling and a **separator key** is posted to the parent, possibly cascading to the root (increasing tree height). Deletion below the fill threshold triggers **redistribution** from a sibling or a **merge** (coalesce); many engines (e.g., InnoDB, Postgres nbtree) use *deferred/lazy* deletion—pages are only reclaimed when empty—trading space for avoiding merge latching. In ARIES/IM, SMOs are made atomic with respect to recovery via logging and (historically) nested top actions.

**Latch coupling (crabbing) and B-link trees.** Traversal safety uses **latch coupling**: acquire child latch before releasing parent; "safe node" optimizations release ancestors early when the child cannot split/merge. **Lehman–Yao B-link trees** (1981) add a **right-sibling pointer** and **high key** to every node: a split first makes the new right sibling reachable via the link, then posts to the parent, so a concurrent reader that lands on a too-small node simply *follows the right-link*. This allows readers to proceed with at most one latch at a time—PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman–Yao variant with Lanin–Shasha-style deletion.

**Key compression and page layout.** **Prefix truncation** stores the common prefix of a page's keys once; **suffix truncation** (Bayer & Unterauer, prefix B-trees) chooses the *shortest separator* that distinguishes split halves when posting to the parent, raising interior fan-out and lowering height. The **slotted page** layout (indirection vector + heap area) permits in-page compaction without changing record slots referenced by indexes.

**Latch-free variant.** The **Bw-tree** (Levandoski et al.) replaces latching entirely with delta records appended via CAS on a **mapping table**, with log-structured page storage—relevant as the modern contrast to latch crabbing.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**Core protocol and the blocking problem.** The coordinator sends PREPARE; each participant force-writes a *prepared* log record (making its vote durable and surrendering unilateral abort rights), votes YES/NO; the coordinator force-writes the global COMMIT/ABORT decision, then broadcasts it; participants write their outcome and ACK. 2PC is a blocking protocol: a participant in the **prepared (in-doubt) window** that loses the coordinator must hold locks until the outcome is learned—the classic availability cost formalized by the impossibility of non-blocking commit under coordinator + participant failure with no extra assumptions.

**Presumed Abort (PA) and Presumed Commit (PC).** These are logging/message optimizations (Mohan, Lindsay, Obermarck). **Presumed abort**: absence of a coordinator log record means abort; the coordinator need not force the abort record nor collect abort ACKs, and read-only participants can answer READ-ONLY to PREPARE and drop out of phase two entirely. PA is the de facto standard (adopted in the X/Open **XA** interface). **Presumed commit** inverts the presumption to cheapen the commit path (no commit ACKs) but requires the coordinator to force a *collecting/initiation* record before prepare, so missing state can safely be presumed committed.

**Termination/recovery mechanisms beyond the basics.** The **cooperative termination protocol** lets an in-doubt participant query *other participants*: if any has committed/aborted or has not prepared, the outcome is resolvable without the coordinator. **Three-Phase Commit (3PC, Skeen)** inserts a *pre-commit* state to make commit non-blocking under a synchronous, no-partition model—but it is unsafe under partitions, which is why practice instead uses **Paxos Commit** (Gray & Lamport 2006): each participant's vote is decided by a Paxos instance across 2F+1 acceptors, making the commit decision itself fault-tolerant; replicated-coordinator 2PC over Raft (e.g., Spanner's 2PC over Paxos groups, TiDB/Percolator-style over Raft) is the production form of this idea.

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport scalar clocks.** Each process keeps a counter; increment on local events, piggyback on messages, and on receive set C := max(C, C_msg) + 1. This guarantees the **clock condition**: e → f (happened-before) ⇒ C(e) < C(f). The converse fails—scalar clocks give a consistent total order (with PID tiebreak) but cannot *detect* concurrency. Used for totally ordering operations, e.g., Lamport's mutual exclusion and deterministic tiebreaks in replicated logs.

**Vector clocks.** Each of N processes keeps an N-vector; component-wise max on receive plus local increment. Vector clocks **characterize causality exactly**: V(e) < V(f) ⟺ e → f, and incomparable vectors identify concurrent events. This exactness (Charron-Bost showed Θ(N) size is necessary) underlies conflict detection in replicated stores. **Version vectors** are the per-object replica-indexed variant for detecting conflicting writes; **dotted version vectors** (Preguiça et al., used in Riak) add a discrete "dot" for the latest event, fixing sibling explosion under concurrent client writes through the same server.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC (Kulkarni, Demirbas et al. 2014) combines physical time pt with a logical component l (and counter c): timestamps respect happened-before like Lamport clocks while staying within bounded drift of physical NTP time, are fixed-size, and allow meaningful "snapshot at wall time t" reads. **CockroachDB** uses HLC for MVCC timestamps and uncertainty intervals (contrast: Spanner's **TrueTime** is *bounded physical* time with explicit ε and commit-wait, not a logical clock—useful foil, not a member of this class).

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Strict read/write quorums (R + W > N).** In Dynamo-style replication over N replicas, requiring read quorum R and write quorum W with **R + W > N** guarantees every read quorum intersects the latest write quorum (and W > N/2 orders writes). Version resolution uses vector clocks or last-write-wins; **read repair** and **anti-entropy via Merkle trees** converge stale replicas. Note the precise guarantee: quorum intersection yields *a* latest-acknowledged version visibility, not linearizability by itself (concurrent in-flight writes can expose non-monotonic reads without extra care—cf. Cassandra's lack of strict linearizability outside LWT/Paxos).

**Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff.** Dynamo's **sloppy quorum** satisfies W on the first N *healthy* nodes on the preference-list walk, not the canonical home set; a stand-in node stores a **hint** and performs **hinted handoff** to the home replica when it recovers. This trades intersection guarantees (two sloppy quorums may not overlap, so even R+W>N can read stale data during failures) for write availability—an explicit AP choice.

**Majority quorums in consensus, and Flexible Paxos.** Paxos/Raft use **majority quorums** so any two quorums intersect, ensuring at most one value is chosen and a new leader's quorum contains the latest committed entry. **Flexible Paxos (FPaxos, Howard et al. 2016)** proves the real requirement is only that *phase-1 (leader-election) quorums intersect phase-2 (replication) quorums*—Q1 + Q2 > N—not Q2 with itself; e.g., N=5 with Q2=2, Q1=4 gives cheap steady-state commits at the price of expensive elections. **Grid quorums** and **witness replicas** (vote-only members, as in Spanner witnesses) are further weight/topology refinements of the same intersection algebra.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery.** (i) **Analysis**: scan forward from the last checkpoint, rebuilding the **Dirty Page Table** (with recLSNs) and **Transaction Table** (loser transactions with lastLSNs). (ii) **Redo**: *repeat history*—from min(recLSN), reapply every logged update (including losers' updates and CLRs) where pageLSN < record LSN, restoring the exact pre-crash state. (iii) **Undo**: roll back losers in reverse LSN order, writing **CLRs** with undoNextLSN so that a crash during recovery never re-undoes work (idempotent, bounded undo). Repeating history is what makes fine-grained (record-level) locking and partial rollbacks via **savepoints** recoverable.

**Fuzzy checkpointing.** Rather than flushing all dirty pages (sharp checkpoint), a **fuzzy checkpoint** logs begin/end checkpoint records containing the DPT and ATT snapshots while normal processing continues; the master record points to the latest completed checkpoint. Redo starts at the minimum recLSN in the logged DPT, so checkpoint cost is decoupled from buffer-pool size. InnoDB's analogue is incremental flushing governed by the gap between the current LSN and the **checkpoint LSN** against redo-log capacity.

**Shadow paging / copy-on-write recovery.** The System R approach and modern descendants avoid in-place update: writes go to fresh pages, and commit atomically swaps the root of a page-table/tree. **LMDB** commits by atomically updating a meta page pointing to a new B+tree root; **SQLite rollback-journal mode** inversely preserves before-images in a journal and replays them on recovery (its **WAL mode** flips to redo-style with periodic **checkpoint** merging of the -wal file into the main database). Shadow paging gives O(1) recovery (no redo/undo scan) but suffers write amplification, clustering loss, and page-table commit contention—exactly the trade ARIES' steal/no-force buffer policy was designed to beat.

**Torn-write and media recovery.** Recovery correctness presumes readable pages: page **checksums** detect corruption; FPW/doublewrite (§1) repair torn pages; **media recovery** = restore backup + roll forward archived WAL to a target LSN/time (PITR), the same redo machinery reused at a different granularity.

---

**Synthesis.** A single spine connects all eight areas: durability and ordering are reduced to an append-only totally ordered log (WAL → LSM memtable WAL → 2PC force-writes → Raft/Paxos replicated logs), visibility is reduced to comparisons over versions/timestamps (MVCC snapshots, Lamport/vector/HLC ordering), and safety under failure is reduced to intersection and idempotence arguments (quorum intersection, pageLSN redo tests, CLR-bounded undo, presumed-outcome logging).

Answer: The brief above covers all eight areas with ≥3 named mechanisms each — (1) WAL: ARIES physiological logging with LSNs/CLRs, group commit, full-page writes vs. InnoDB doublewrite buffer; (2) MVCC: PostgreSQL xmin/xmax+VACUUM/HOT, InnoDB undo-log read views+purge, SSI rw-antidependency detection (plus Hekaton); (3) LSM: memtable/SSTable+tombstones, leveled vs. size-tiered/universal compaction, Bloom filters+fence pointers (Monkey); (4) B+trees: split/merge SMOs, latch crabbing vs. Lehman–Yao B-link right-links, prefix/suffix truncation (plus Bw-tree); (5) 2PC: presumed abort/presumed commit, cooperative termination, 3PC vs. Paxos Commit/2PC-over-Raft; (6) logical clocks: Lamport, vector/dotted version vectors, Hybrid Logical Clocks; (7) quorums: strict R+W>N, sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, majority/Flexible Paxos quorum intersection; (8) crash recovery: ARIES analysis–redo–undo with repeating history, fuzzy checkpoints, shadow paging/copy-on-write (LMDB, SQLite) plus media/PITR recovery.

response.content:
# Write-Ahead Logging

**ARIES physiological logging with LSNs and CLRs.** Each log record gets a monotonically increasing Log Sequence Number. Records are physiological: physical with respect to the page (identified by pageID), logical within it (e.g., "delete the record with key k from this page"), which keeps redo cheap and tolerates intra-page reorganization. Every page carries a pageLSN, the LSN of the last record applied to it. Two invariants govern everything:

- **WAL rule**: a dirty page may be written to disk only after all log records up to its pageLSN are durable (pageLSN ≤ flushedLSN). This is what permits a steal buffer policy.
- **Commit rule (force-log-at-commit)**: a transaction is reported committed only after its commit record is durable. This permits no-force page writes.

Rollback writes Compensation Log Records. A CLR is redo-only and carries an undoNextLSN pointing past the record it compensated. Invariant: CLRs are never undone, so undo work is bounded even across repeated crashes during recovery. Each transaction's records are backward-chained via prevLSN, making selective rollback a list walk.

**Group commit.** Multiple committing transactions share one log fsync. The durability invariant is unchanged, only batched: no transaction is acknowledged until flushedLSN covers its commit LSN. Failure semantics: a crash can lose transactions that executed their commit record write but were never acknowledged, which is correct; the anomaly to avoid is acknowledging before the batched flush, which silently loses committed work. PostgreSQL exposes the trade as `commit_delay`; InnoDB as `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit`, where values other than one deliberately weaken the commit rule and can lose up to a second of acknowledged commits.

**Torn-page protection: full-page writes vs the doublewrite buffer.** Database pages (8 to 16 KB) exceed the device's atomic write unit, so a crash mid-write leaves a page that is half old, half new. Physiological redo applied to a torn page corrupts it, so the invariant is: never apply delta redo to a page whose on-disk image is not some consistent prior version. PostgreSQL's full-page writes log the entire page image on first modification after each checkpoint; redo then replaces rather than patches, making the torn state irrelevant. InnoDB's doublewrite buffer writes dirty pages first to a sequential doublewrite area, fsyncs, then writes them to their home locations. Recovery detects torn home pages by checksum and restores from the doublewrite copy. Full-page writes inflate WAL volume after checkpoints; doublewrite roughly doubles data-page write traffic but keeps the log small.

# MVCC

**PostgreSQL xmin/xmax versioning with VACUUM.** Every tuple version stores the inserting transaction ID (xmin) and deleting/updating one (xmax). Visibility invariant for a snapshot: xmin is committed and not in the snapshot's in-progress set and below its xmax horizon, and the tuple's xmax is absent, aborted, or invisible to the snapshot. Updates create whole new tuple versions, so dead versions accumulate until VACUUM removes those older than the global xmin horizon. Failure semantics: a single long-running transaction pins the horizon and causes unbounded bloat. Transaction IDs are 32-bit and circular, so VACUUM must freeze old tuples; the invariant is that no unfrozen xmin falls more than about two billion XIDs behind the current one. Violating it would flip visibility, so PostgreSQL first warns, then refuses new transactions (wraparound protection shutdown).

**InnoDB undo logs and read views.** InnoDB updates rows in place and writes the prior version to undo logs, with each record carrying a roll pointer chaining to older versions. A read view records the low and high transaction-ID watermarks and the set of active transactions at snapshot time; a reader walks the undo chain until it finds a version whose creator is visible. Purge threads reclaim undo records no longer needed by any read view. Failure semantics mirror PostgreSQL's: a long-running transaction grows the history list, lengthening version chains and slowing every reader, but the bloat lives in undo space rather than the table heap.

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation.** Plain snapshot isolation admits write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint data, and the result is non-serializable. SSI (Cahill et al., implemented in PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE) tracks read-write antidependencies with SIREAD locks, which block nothing. The theorem it relies on: every snapshot-isolation serializability violation contains a "dangerous structure," a pivot transaction with both an incoming and an outgoing rw-antidependency edge to concurrent transactions. Detecting that structure and aborting one participant guarantees serializability. Failure semantics: detection is conservative, so false-positive aborts occur and applications must retry on serialization failures; false negatives never occur.

# LSM Trees

Writes land in a WAL-protected memtable; full memtables become immutable and flush as sorted SSTables. Reads must consult the memtable plus every run that might hold the key, so the design space is governed by compaction.

**Leveled vs size-tiered compaction.** Leveled compaction (RocksDB default) keeps each level beyond the first as a single sorted run of non-overlapping SSTables, with level sizes growing by a fanout factor T. Invariants: within a leveled level, key ranges are disjoint, so a point read touches at most one SSTable per level; level L's size stays within T times level L-1. This minimizes space and read amplification but rewrites data roughly T times per level, so write amplification is T times the number of levels. Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra STCS) merges runs of similar size into larger runs, allowing several overlapping runs per tier: write amplification drops to roughly one rewrite per tier, but reads must check every run and space amplification can transiently approach double the data size during a large merge. Failure semantics for compaction itself are clean because SSTables are immutable: a crashed compaction leaves inputs intact and orphans the partial output, which is garbage-collected via the manifest.

**Bloom filters.** Each SSTable carries a Bloom filter over its keys. Invariant: no false negatives, tunable false-positive rate, so a negative filter answer safely skips the file. They accelerate point lookups only; ordinary Bloom filters cannot serve range scans, which is why prefix Bloom filters exist for bounded-prefix iteration.

**Fence pointers.** Per-block index entries (first key of each block) kept in memory or in the SSTable index block. Invariant: a point read in a sorted run needs at most one data-block read, found by binary search over the fences.

**Tombstones.** Deletes are logical markers merged above older values. The critical invariant: a tombstone may be dropped only when no older version of its key can exist below it, in practice when compaction carries it to the bottom level or can prove no overlap beneath. Dropping it early resurrects deleted data. Range tombstones cover key intervals and must be similarly retained; Cassandra adds gc_grace_seconds so tombstones outlive the repair window, and a node down longer than that window can resurrect deletes cluster-wide.

# B+tree Maintenance

**Latch crabbing.** Descent acquires the child's latch before releasing the parent's, so at most two latches are held and the path stays consistent. For writers, the parent latch is released only once the child is "safe," meaning it cannot split on insert or underflow on delete, which bounds latch scope to the subtree that an SMO could touch. The common optimization descends optimistically with read latches, write-latching only the leaf, and restarts pessimistically if the leaf turns out unsafe.

**B-link trees (Lehman–Yao).** Every node carries a right-sibling pointer and a high key bounding its contents. A split is two-phase: create the right sibling and move keys, then separately insert the separator into the parent. Invariant: between the phases, keys moved right remain reachable by following the right-link whenever the search key exceeds a node's high key. This lets readers hold one latch at a time and never block on splits. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a B-link tree; its failure semantics depend on it, since a crash between split phases leaves an "incomplete split" that is structurally valid, detected by a page flag and completed by the next insertion rather than by recovery.

**Structure modification operations as nested top actions.** In ARIES/IM, a split or merge is logged as a nested top action terminated by a dummy CLR, making the SMO atomic and redo-only: it is never rolled back even if the triggering transaction aborts, because other transactions may already depend on the new structure. Invariant: at every point recovery can observe, the tree is structurally consistent; logical undo of the aborting transaction's insert then proceeds against the new shape. Deletion maintenance in practice uses free-at-empty with deferred page reclamation rather than textbook merge-at-half-full, and deleted pages must not be recycled while any concurrent scan could still hold a pointer to them, which PostgreSQL enforces by stamping deleted pages and recycling only after all potentially-referencing snapshots are gone.

**Suffix truncation of separator keys.** When a leaf splits, the separator posted to the parent needs only enough bytes to distinguish the maximum key of the left sibling from the minimum of the right. Invariant: the separator compares strictly between those two keys. This raises interior-node fanout and shrinks tree height. Prefix compression within pages (storing a shared prefix once) is the complementary intra-node technique; both must be undone logically, never byte-wise, during key comparison.

# Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-pass recovery.** Analysis scans forward from the last checkpoint, rebuilding the Active Transaction Table (loser transactions and their lastLSNs) and the Dirty Page Table (pages possibly dirty, each with a recLSN, the LSN that first dirtied it). Redo starts at the minimum recLSN and repeats history: it reapplies every update, including those of losers, restoring the exact pre-crash state. Idempotence invariant: a record is applied only if its LSN exceeds the page's pageLSN, so partial recovery followed by another crash is safe. Undo then rolls back losers in reverse LSN order across all transactions simultaneously, writing CLRs. The undoNextLSN chain guarantees monotone progress: a crash during undo never redoes undo work. Repeating history is what allows steal/no-force buffering with fine-grained physiological logging.

**Fuzzy checkpoints.** A checkpoint logs begin and end records containing the current ATT and DPT without flushing dirty pages or quiescing transactions. The master record points at the latest complete checkpoint. Invariant: the DPT snapshot bounds the redo start point, so checkpoint frequency trades log-replay length against checkpoint overhead, never correctness. Failure semantics: a crash between begin and end checkpoint records simply falls back to the previous complete checkpoint.

**Shadow paging.** The System R alternative, surviving in copy-on-write engines like LMDB: updates write new pages, and commit atomically installs a new page-table root. Invariant: the single atomic root-pointer swap is the commit point; before it, the old tree is fully intact, so recovery is free of redo and undo entirely. LMDB keeps two root slots selected by transaction ID and relies on one atomic page write. Failure semantics are trivially clean, but the costs explain why ARIES won for general-purpose engines: destroyed physical clustering, garbage collection of superseded pages, and commit serialization through the root, which makes fine-grained concurrent transactions hard. It also still needs torn-write protection for the root page itself, typically via checksummed dual roots.

**Summary of findings.** WAL correctness reduces to two ordering invariants (log-before-page, log-before-ack) plus torn-page defense. MVCC designs differ in where garbage lives (heap vs undo) but share the horizon problem, and SSI upgrades snapshot isolation via dangerous-structure detection. LSM correctness hinges on tombstone retention and manifest-driven atomicity of immutable file sets, with leveled vs tiered compaction trading write against read and space amplification. B+tree concurrency safety comes from crabbing or B-link right-links, and crash safety from logging SMOs as atomic nested top actions. ARIES ties it together with repeat-history redo, CLR-bounded undo, and fuzzy checkpoints, while shadow paging trades all recovery logic for clustering and concurrency costs.

response.content:
## Two-phase commit (2PC) and its variants

**Baseline protocol and blocking behavior.** 2PC solves atomic commitment: all participants decide commit or abort, with agreement, validity, and termination. The coordinator sends PREPARE. Each participant force-writes a prepared log record and votes YES, or votes NO and aborts unilaterally. The coordinator force-writes the decision and broadcasts it. The protocol assumes a crash-recovery failure model with stable storage. Participants that crash replay their log on restart. The core weakness is the in-doubt window. A participant that has voted YES has surrendered its right to abort. If the coordinator then fails, the participant must hold locks until the coordinator recovers. This blocking is fundamental, not an implementation flaw. No atomic commitment protocol can be non-blocking in the presence of communication failures or partitions, which is a corollary of the Two Generals impossibility. Skeen and Stonebraker proved that any protocol whose state machine allows a crash in a state adjacent to both commit and abort outcomes can block.

**Presumed abort and presumed commit.** These are the R* logging optimizations of Mohan, Lindsay, and Obermarck. In presumed abort, the coordinator writes no abort record and forgets aborted transactions immediately. When a recovering participant inquires about an unknown transaction, the coordinator answers abort by presumption. This removes the forced abort record, the abort ACKs, and enables the read-only optimization: a read-only participant votes READ-ONLY, writes nothing, and is excluded from phase two. Presumed commit inverts the presumption. The coordinator force-writes a collecting record naming the participants before sending PREPARE, so that missing state after a coordinator crash safely means commit. It saves forced commit records and commit ACKs at participants, at the cost of that extra initial force-write. Presumed abort is the variant standardized in practice because most distributed transactions historically had read-only participants. Neither variant changes blocking behavior or the failure model. They reduce forced log writes and message count only.

**Cooperative termination protocol.** When an in-doubt participant times out waiting for the coordinator, it queries the other participants, whose identities are carried in the PREPARE message. If any peer has received the decision, or any peer has not yet voted and therefore aborts, the in-doubt participant resolves. The protocol reduces the probability of blocking but does not eliminate it. If the coordinator crashes after all participants have prepared and before any has learned the outcome, all participants are in-doubt and the group still blocks until coordinator recovery.

**Three-phase commit (3PC).** Skeen's 3PC inserts a pre-commit state between prepared and committed, removing the forbidden adjacency of uncertain and committed states. With a termination protocol that elects a new coordinator, 3PC is non-blocking, but only in a synchronous system with fail-stop crashes and no network partitions. Under a partition, two sides can elect separate coordinators and decide differently, violating atomicity. 3PC also costs a third round of forced writes and messages in the failure-free path. E3PC by Keidar and Dolev repairs the partition unsafety with quorum-based recovery: only a connected majority may move the decision forward, which trades back some availability for safety.

**Paxos Commit.** Gray and Lamport replace the single coordinator decision with one Paxos consensus instance per participant vote, run over 2F+1 acceptors. The transaction commits iff every instance chooses YES. Safety holds in the asynchronous crash-recovery model, and the protocol is non-blocking whenever F+1 acceptors are reachable, so coordinator failure no longer strands prepared participants. With acceptors co-located with the leader and phase one pre-executed, the failure-free latency matches 2PC in message delays while sending roughly F times more messages. 2PC is exactly the degenerate case F=0, which makes precise the claim that 2PC's blocking is the price of zero replication of the commit decision. Liveness, as with all Paxos variants, requires partial synchrony per FLP. Modern systems such as Spanner take the related route of making the coordinator itself a Paxos-replicated state machine, which removes the single point of failure without changing the 2PC message pattern between shards.

## Logical clocks

**Lamport clocks.** A scalar counter per process, incremented on local events, piggybacked on messages, and set to max(local, received)+1 on delivery. They satisfy the clock condition in one direction only: a happens-before b implies C(a) < C(b). The converse fails, so Lamport timestamps cannot detect concurrency. Breaking ties with process IDs yields a total order consistent with causality, which is what Lamport's mutual exclusion algorithm and timestamp-ordered state machine replication rely on. Failure model is irrelevant to correctness of the ordering itself, but the induced total order delays delivery until all lower-timestamped messages are known, which stalls under a single crashed peer without failure detection.

**Vector clocks.** Due independently to Fidge and Mattern, a vector of N counters characterizes causality exactly: VC(a) < VC(b) iff a happened-before b, and incomparable vectors mean concurrent events. This bidirectional property is what enables causal broadcast, causal consistency (as in COPS-style systems), and conflict detection in optimistic replication. Charron-Bost proved the O(N) size is necessary to capture causality exactly, so the space cost cannot be optimized away in general. A terminology point that matters for precision: version vectors track causality between object versions with one entry per replica, while vector clocks track events with one entry per process. Conflating them causes sizing bugs when clients outnumber replicas.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** Kulkarni, Demirbas, et al. combine a physical component l and a logical counter c in constant space. The update rules keep l at the maximum physical time observed, bumping c to preserve monotonicity when physical time has not advanced. HLC satisfies the Lamport clock condition while guaranteeing l stays within the clock synchronization bound ε of true physical time. This gives causally consistent snapshots addressable by wall-clock time without blocking, unlike Spanner's TrueTime, which achieves external consistency by commit-wait, deliberately sleeping out the uncertainty interval. CockroachDB uses HLC for transaction timestamps, and MongoDB uses it for causal consistency in sessions. HLC tolerates NTP-level drift but its bound degrades if ε is violated, so it inherits a timing assumption that pure logical clocks do not have.

**Dotted version vectors (DVV).** Preguiça, Baquero, et al. address sibling explosion in get/put key-value stores like Riak. A dot (replica, counter) names one specific write, kept separate from the causal context vector that summarizes what the writer had seen. This lets a server distinguish two writes it coordinated itself from genuinely concurrent client writes, so concurrent updates through the same server no longer generate spurious siblings, and the number of retained siblings is bounded by the degree of true concurrency. Plain version vectors with server IDs lose updates in this scenario, and per-client IDs grow unboundedly. DVVs fix both.

## Quorum systems

**Strict quorums, R+W>N.** With N replicas, read quorum R, and write quorum W, R+W>N guarantees every read quorum intersects every write quorum, so a read observes at least one copy of the most recently completed write. W>N/2 additionally makes write quorums pairwise intersecting, which is needed to order writes by version. Intersection alone does not give linearizability. A read concurrent with a write can return the new value while a later read returns the old one. The ABD algorithm (Attiya, Bar-Noy, Dolev) closes this gap by having readers write back the highest timestamped value to a write quorum before returning, yielding a linearizable register in an asynchronous crash-stop model with up to N minus quorum-size failures. Dynamo-style stores exposing tunable R and W without read write-back therefore do not provide linearizability even at R+W>N, a point Kleppmann's analyses make precisely.

**Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff.** Dynamo's availability mechanism assembles the quorum from the first N healthy nodes on the consistent-hashing preference list rather than the designated home set. A write accepted by a substitute node carries a hint and is handed off to the home node when it recovers. Because the quorum membership itself shifts during failures, read and write quorums are no longer guaranteed to intersect, so R+W>N provides no recency guarantee at all. The system degrades explicitly to eventual consistency, repaired by hinted handoff, read repair, and anti-entropy with Merkle trees, with concurrent versions detected by version vectors and surfaced as siblings. The trade is deliberate: write availability and durability under partitions in exchange for consistency, per the CAP trade-off.

**Flexible Paxos (FPaxos).** Howard, Malkhi, and Spiegelman observed that Paxos does not need all quorums to intersect. Only every phase-1 (leader election) quorum Q1 must intersect every phase-2 (replication) quorum Q2, so Q1+Q2>N suffices, and phase-2 quorums need not intersect each other. Since phase 2 is the steady state and phase 1 runs only on leader change, one can shrink Q2 (lower replication latency, higher throughput) at the cost of a larger Q1 (more expensive, less available recovery). Grid quorums instantiate this with Q2 as a row and Q1 as a column of a node matrix. The generalization underlies follow-ons like WPaxos and informs multi-datacenter quorum placement.

**Byzantine quorum systems.** Malkhi and Reiter's dissemination and masking quorum systems extend intersection requirements for arbitrary faults. With N=3f+1 and quorums of 2f+1, any two quorums intersect in at least f+1 nodes, guaranteeing at least one correct node in every intersection. This is the quorum logic inside PBFT and its descendants, and it explains the 3f+1 lower bound for Byzantine agreement without signatures. Classic metrics for comparing all these constructions are Naor and Wool's load, capacity, and fault tolerance, under which majority quorums have high fault tolerance but load 1/2, while grid-style systems lower load to O(1/√N) at reduced availability.

**Cross-cutting precision notes.** Quorum intersection gives safety in asynchronous crash-recovery models, but liveness always requires enough reachable replicas. 2PC composes with quorums in modern designs: each shard is a quorum-replicated state machine, and 2PC runs across shard leaders, so coordinator blocking is masked by consensus-based leader failover rather than eliminated in the Skeen sense.
